lessons.title: Lesson 1: Understanding game-day nerves
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Notice your own signs of nerves and see them as energy you can manage.
This lesson builds toward: Thinking back to a recent big game, you will describe your own body signs and thoughts of nerves and when they start, naming at least two body signs and one thought.
Before a big game, your heart beats faster, your hands may sweat and your stomach may flutter. This is your body getting ready to perform. A little of it helps; too much can make you tense or rushed.
Everyone feels it, including pros. The skill is not to make nerves disappear, but to notice them and bring them down to a level that helps you.
Start by noticing. What do you feel in your body, what thoughts show up, and when do they start? Writing it down makes it easier to manage.
Words to know:
- Nerves: the body's natural reaction before something important: faster heart, sweaty hands, butterflies.
- Arousal level: how revved up you feel, from very calm to very wound up.
Try it now: Think about your last big game. Write three body signs and two thoughts you had before it started, and when they began.
You can now notice your own signs of nerves and describe them.

check.q: What is a flutter in your stomach before a game?
options: A sign you should not play
Your body getting ready to perform
check.why: These body signs are your body getting ready; the skill is to manage them.

check.q: You want to start managing your nerves. What do you do first?
options: Write down what you feel, think and when it starts
Try to make the nerves disappear
check.why: Noticing and writing it down makes nerves easier to manage.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Box breathing: a 60-second reset
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use box breathing to calm your body in about a minute.
This lesson builds toward: Before or during practice, you will demonstrate box breathing for four rounds, using equal counts of four, or slow breathing without holds if holding feels uncomfortable.
Slow breathing is one of the fastest ways to calm your body. Box breathing is simple: breathe in for a count of four, hold for four, breathe out for four, hold for four. Repeat four times.
You can do it on the bench, at the free-throw line with shorter counts, in the locker room or before a test. Practice it when you are calm so it works when you are nervous.
If holding your breath feels uncomfortable, skip the holds and just breathe in slowly and out even more slowly. Stop if you feel dizzy.
Step by step:
- Breathe in through your nose for 4.
- Hold for 4.
- Breathe out slowly for 4.
- Hold for 4.
- Repeat 4 rounds.
Words to know:
- Box breathing: breathing in, holding, breathing out and holding for equal counts, like the four sides of a box.
Try it now: Do four rounds of box breathing right now. Rate how tense you feel from 1 to 10 before and after.
You can now use box breathing to calm your body in about a minute.

check.q: How many rounds of box breathing does the lesson suggest?
check.why: Breathe in 4, hold 4, out 4, hold 4, and repeat four times.

check.q: You feel dizzy during box breathing. What do you do?
options: Keep going for ten more rounds
check.why: The lesson says stop if you feel dizzy.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Cue words and self-talk
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write three cue words and turn negative self-talk into useful instructions.
This lesson builds toward: Given a negative thought you often have, you will write three cue words that tell your body what to do, with each cue word one to three words long and about something you control.
Self-talk is what you say to yourself in your head. "Don't miss" puts the picture of missing in your mind. "Smooth release, follow through" tells your body what to do.
Cue words are one to three words that point your focus: "eyes up", "quick feet", "next play", "strong and tall". Pick words about what you control, not about the score.
An AI assistant can help. Try: "I'm a volleyball server. When I'm nervous I think 'don't serve into the net'. Give me five short cue words that tell me what to do instead." Pick the ones that feel like you.
Step by step:
- Write a negative thought you often have.
- Ask: what do I want my body to do instead?
- Turn it into 1-3 words.
- Pick three cue words and practice saying them.
Words to know:
- Self-talk: the words you say to yourself in your head.
- Cue word: a short word or phrase that points your focus to what to do.
Try it now: Write one negative thought you have in games. Use an AI assistant to get five cue words that tell you what to do instead. Choose your top three.
You can now write cue words and turn negative self-talk into useful instructions.

options: A long speech before a game
One to three words that point your focus
check.why: Cue words are short phrases like "eyes up" that point your focus.

check.q: Before a penalty kick you often think "don't miss". What do you change it to?
check.why: Useful self-talk tells your body what to do, not what to avoid.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Building a pre-game routine
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a pre-game routine with times and steps you control.
This lesson builds toward: Using your game-day schedule, you will write a pre-game routine from the night before to the first whistle, with only steps you control, a breathing reset, your cue words, and timing checked with your coach.
A routine is a set of steps you do the same way before every game. It gives your mind something familiar to hold on to, so you feel ready no matter the opponent.
A simple routine: the night before (pack bag, sleep routine), game-day meal, arrival, warm-up, a one-minute breathing reset, your cue words, and a focus on your first job in the game.
Keep the steps about things you control. Superstitions are fine for fun, but the routine should still work if you forget your lucky socks. Check timing with your coach so it fits the team warm-up.
Step by step:
- List what you do from the night before to the first whistle.
- Add a breathing reset and your cue words.
- Name your first job in the game.
- Keep only steps you control.
- Check it fits your team's warm-up.
Words to know:
- Routine: steps you repeat the same way each time.
- Controllable: something you can choose or change yourself, like effort or preparation.
Try it now: Ask an AI assistant to turn your list of pre-game steps into a clean timeline from the night before to the first whistle. Edit it so it matches your real game day.
You can now write a pre-game routine built on steps you control.

options: Steps you do the same way before every game
A new plan for each opponent
check.why: A routine is the same set of steps every game, giving your mind something familiar.

check.q: Your routine depends on wearing one lucky shirt. What do you do?
options: Skip the game if you forget the shirt
Make sure the routine still works with steps you control
Ask the coach to bring a spare
check.why: Keep the steps about things you control so the routine works anyway.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Resetting after a mistake
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use a three-step reset to move on from a mistake during a game.
This lesson builds toward: After a mistake during a game or practice, you will use the three-step reset: release, reset and refocus, completing all three steps before the next play and saving the review for after the game.
Every athlete makes mistakes. What matters is how fast you move to the next play. Dwelling on a mistake often causes the next one.
A three-step reset: 1. Release: a physical action that says "done", like wiping your hands, touching your shoe or a breath out. 2. Reset: one slow breath. 3. Refocus: say your cue word for the next play.
After the game, not during it, look back at the mistake to learn from it with your coach or film. In the moment, the only job is the next play.
Step by step:
- Release: one physical action that means "done".
- Reset: one slow breath.
- Refocus: say your next-play cue word.
- Learn from it after the game, not during.
Words to know:
- Reset: a quick routine to clear your mind and get ready for the next moment.
- Next-play mindset: focusing on what is coming, not what just happened.
Try it now: Choose your release action and your next-play cue word. At your next practice, use the three-step reset after every mistake and count how many times you used it.
You can now use a three-step reset to move on quickly from a mistake.

check.q: What is the release step of the mistake reset?
options: Replaying the mistake in your head
check.why: Release is a physical action like wiping your hands or touching your shoe.

check.q: You just dropped a pass. What is your job right now?
options: Release, take one slow breath and say your next-play cue word
check.why: In the moment, the only job is the next play; learn from it after the game.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: When it is more than nerves: getting support
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Identify the signs that stress needs real support and name who to contact.
This lesson builds toward: Given signs that stress is more than nerves, you will identify the warning signs and name who to contact, including 988 and 911, naming at least two trusted people and the right number for a crisis and an emergency.
Mental skills help with normal pressure. But sometimes stress is bigger: you feel down most days, lose interest in things you liked, can't sleep or eat, feel hopeless, or think about hurting yourself. That is not a weakness, and it is not something a breathing drill or an AI chatbot can fix.
Reach out to a real person: a parent or trusted adult, your coach, your athletic trainer, a school counselor, your team doctor or a licensed mental health professional. Many schools and colleges offer free counseling.
If you or someone you know is in crisis or thinking about suicide in the United States, call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org. It is free and open 24/7. In an emergency, call 911.
Step by step:
- Notice the signs that it is more than nerves.
- Tell a trusted adult, coach, athletic trainer or counselor.
- Find your school's counseling service.
- In crisis: call or text 988. In an emergency: 911.
Words to know:
- Licensed mental health professional: a trained, licensed counselor, psychologist or therapist.
- 988 Lifeline: the free US Suicide and Crisis Lifeline: call, text or chat 24/7.
Official sources:
- 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline
Try it now: Final task: write your one-page pre-game routine card with your breathing reset, three cue words and three-step mistake reset. At the bottom, write the names of two people you could talk to and how to reach your school's counseling service. Share the card with your coach.
You can now use your mental performance routine and know when and where to get real support.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Pre-game time-line Steps are missing times, or depend on things outside the athlete's control. A time-line from the night before to the first whistle with only controllable steps, checked with the coach. Names the athlete's first job in the game and fits the team warm-up exactly. Breathing reset No breathing reset, or the counts are unclear. Box breathing (or slow breathing without holds) is on the card at a set point and practiced at two practices. Includes a shorter version for in-game moments like the free-throw line. Cue words Fewer than three cue words, or they are about the score or what to avoid. Three cue words of one to three words each, about what the athlete controls. Each cue word replaces a named negative thought the athlete often has. Mistake reset One or more of the three steps is missing. Release, reset and refocus are written with the athlete's own action and cue word. The athlete reports using it at practice and notes what to review after the game. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Which is a sign that stress needs real support?
options: A fast heartbeat at the start line
Sweaty hands at the free-throw line
check.why: Feeling down or hopeless most days is more than normal nerves.

check.q: A friend texts that they are thinking about suicide. In the United States, what do you do?
options: Tell them to try box breathing
Ask an AI chatbot what to do
Tell a trusted adult right away and share 988, or call 911 if they are in danger now
check.why: A real person must help; 988 is the crisis line and 911 is for emergencies.
